doc.title: Ted Piltzecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 10, 2019

title: No single aha moment: early listening and the drum corps
summary: He had no defining moment; he recalls his mother's Al Hirt records, his sister's Bill Evans and Miles, and the drum corps and bugle that kept him off the streets.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Did you have an aha moment as a kid, like with music, that this could be something that I really want to pursue? Something that occurred, a recording or seeing somebody?

I think it would be nice to say yes and like many artists can say, “When I was in fourth grade somebody came through town and I was knocked out and never forgot it.” I don’t think I ever had one of those. And I’m a little maybe different from a lot of other great — not great but other artists, that I just sort of did it and it was something I did pretty well and I — okay, well I guess I’ll go to music school and I just meandered into music school and then I sort of got into it. I mean I didn’t really have a moment in my childhood — my parents, my mother is from New Orleans, she used to play some Al Hirt songs when I was younger and that was — I used to listen to that and Louis Prima, and my sister who was older came with a Bill Evans album and I played it, and Miles, and I thought man, this music is from space, man. I couldn’t understand it at all, especially Bill on “Blue In Green.” And I said it just sounds so, it didn’t make any sense to me. You know some people listen to Shostakovich or Schoenberg or something, you’re not quite ready for it. And it wasn’t until years later that of course “Blue In Green” has never been my favorite song to play, but I didn’t have one of those early childhood moments. I went to Eastman and when I got to Eastman I heard a lot of great music. In fact, maybe one other thing. I had a high school choir director that, we played not showy music but we sang Brahms and you know, it was a really wonderful experience. I was the president of the choir, had the worst voice. But it was an engagement of music making that I sort of remember. That

was a really formative time I think artistically and aesthetically. Before that I played in a drum corps and that basically was functioning to get me off the streets and keep me out of trouble, which it did. I’m very thankful for that. Some of the guys that were hanging around at the time got into trouble. So my mom said get away from this gang, join the drum corps. There were no more drums left so they gave me a bugle and I played the bugle and then I got to high school and I played the trumpet, seemed to be the next thing, and all of a sudden I’m a trumpet major at Eastman.
